synthesis.headline: Longwave dipole rotates east: deep central-US trough takes over, a fresh Northwest ridge builds behind it, and Polo's moisture primes a multi-day Southwest-to-South-Central flood regime
synthesis.narrative:
The autumn longwave pattern that has framed the continent all week has swung a notch eastward, and that rotation is today's organizing story. The deep western trough that anchored the Pacific Northwest and northern Rockies yesterday has dropped into the interior and now sits as a deep, slightly negatively tilted longwave trough over the central United States (heights near 558-564 dam over the central Plains). Behind it a large-amplitude ridge has rebuilt into the Pacific Northwest and western Canada (588-594 dam), while a separate ridge holds over the Gulf of Mexico and the old eastern feature has fully detached into a genuine cutoff low offshore the mid-Atlantic (near 575-576 dam). At the surface this appears as a broad low/frontal complex from the central Plains into the Great Lakes with a cold front trailing into the southern Plains, a departing coastal cyclone off New Jersey, and — in Canada — a sprawling low complex over central and eastern Canada (a 999 hPa center near the Great Lakes/Ontario, a 982 hPa low toward Hudson Bay) opposed by a strong 1033 hPa high over the James Bay/eastern Hudson Bay area. That high's western flank packs the isobars into a corridor of strong winds across northern Quebec and Labrador, the most vigorous surface gradient on the Canadian map.

Today's centers of action are stacked along the tropical-moisture pipeline rather than along a severe-weather axis. The main event is a multi-day heavy-rain and flash-flood regime: major Hurricane Polo (100 kt, near Cabo San Lazaro) is pumping deep tropical moisture into the Southwest, Great Basin, and central/southern Rockies, with WPC hanging a Moderate Risk for excessive rainfall and considerable flash flooding flagged for New Mexico and western Texas Monday through Wednesday. The WPC extended discussion carries this forward with above-average confidence: the southern-stream closed low and its wavy fronts crawl slowly from the Southwest into the South-Central and then East-Central U.S. through late week, wedged between ridges over the Southwest and Southeast, with a Day 4 (Thursday) Southern Plains Moderate ERO and anomalously large risk areas beyond. Second, the powerful Nor'easter near New Jersey brings coastal flooding, rip currents, strong winds and heavy rain to the Mid-Atlantic and Northeast through Monday before weakening into the Gulf of Maine on Tuesday. Third, a northern-Plains low spreads a Slight Risk for excessive rainfall into the Upper Midwest. Severe weather is a genuine non-event today — SPC has no Day 1 severe areas and no mesoscale discussions — though a severe threat is advertised over the Southern Plains by Wednesday as the system organizes.

Upstairs the amplified longwave configuration — Northwest ridge, deep central trough, offshore Atlantic cutoff — is not a clean Rex or omega block but does have reduced downstream progression. The Air Mass RGB shows a broad dry, warm upper airmass under the western ridging and a sharp airmass boundary arcing southwest-to-northeast from the central Plains into the Great Lakes, marking the implied jet corridor (60-80 kt along the trough's southern and eastern flank) that separates the dry western air from deep tropical green streaming north out of the Gulf, with clusters of deep convection already firing over the Tennessee and lower Mississippi valleys. The central trough retains a translational (progressive) character, so it will move; the offshore cutoff, by contrast, will meander or retrogress rather than clear cleanly, a tendency the strengthened negative NAO (7-day mean near -1.01) supports. The regime question remains the one we have tracked all week, and the ensemble pair settles it in the same direction: the 6-10 day (Oct 3-7) still holds a mid-latitude ridge over the interior West with a strong warm signal over the Northwest and northern Great Basin, but the 8-14 day (Oct 5-11) shrinks and relocates that ridge, pulling its core southwest to the Four Corners and northern Mexico while western Canada, the northern Rockies, and the northern Plains go near-normal to weakly negative and a deep trough anchors over the Canadian Arctic and Hudson Bay. That is geographic contraction and poleward retreat of the amplification, not a rebuild of a durable western ridge over the lower 48 — a continuing regime transition, and the reason the flood regime stays wedged and slow.
synthesis.climate_context: The ONI table's tabulated progression climbs out of last winter's weak La Niña, crosses positive in spring, and reaches roughly +1.80 by JJA 2026, so its "current" cool label lags its own data — late September sits in moderate-to-strong El Niño territory. The tropics fit that state with a textbook basin split just past the seasonal peak: the Atlantic is comparatively quiet (Tropical Depression Fay near the Azores and a high-probability but oceanic development east-northeast of Bermuda, neither a continental concern), while the East Pacific is hyperactive, running Hurricanes Polo and Nolo, Tropical Storm Rachel, and another likely depression east-southeast of Hawaii. The North American Monsoon is in its fading late-season phase but still supplies the Pacific-and-Gulf moisture overlap that, joined to Polo's tropical connection, fuels the Southwest-to-South-Central rains into the coming week. Late-season severe weather stays in its expected ridge-periphery, Southern Plains mode rather than deep-Plains outbreaks. Teleconnections are only a weak warm-season cross-check but align with the height field: the modestly negative PNA is consistent with the absence of a durable mid-latitude western ridge, and the deepening negative NAO supports the stalling eastern cutoff and the emerging high-latitude Arctic amplification.
synthesis.regional_notes: SPC has no Day 1 severe areas and no mesoscale discussions in the past six hours. Non-severe scattered to isolated thunderstorms are expected over the Northern Plains on modest CAPE and a reinvigorating overnight low-level jet, and numerous showers/storms over southeast California into western Arizona ahead of a mid-level shortwave, though widespread cloud and weak mid-level lapse rates cap the instability there. The near-term flood focus is the Southwest/Great Basin/Rockies, with the New Mexico and western Texas flash-flood threat most acute. In Canada, watch the strong wind corridor along the western flank of the Hudson Bay/James Bay high into northern Quebec and Labrador, plus the BC coastal front beneath the 1008 hPa offshore low. In Mexico, Polo is a direct Baja/Northwest Mexico landfall and heavy-rain threat, and Tropical Storm Rachel is active south-southwest of Acapulco.

sources.title: Surface Analysis
sources.summary: This 0900Z 28 September 2026 WPC surface analysis shows a sprawling high pressure regime across much of the central and eastern CONUS, with a 1028 mb high centered over the upper Great Lakes/Ontario region and a 1024 mb high anchored off the Pacific Northwest coast, collectively producing a slack pressure gradient across the interior West and central Plains where isobars are widely spaced. The most dynamically active region is the central and southern Rockies eastward through the southern Plains, where a 1009 mb low over the central Rockies feeds a cold front extending southeastward into the southern Plains and a warm front or stationary boundary running eastward, with the frontal convergence zone and backed surface winds in the warm sector over Oklahoma, Kansas, and Texas implying a focus for lift and moisture return from the Gulf, consistent with dewpoints in the upper 60s to low 70s F visible in that sector. Hurricane Polo is annotated off the Mexican Pacific coast with a note indicating maximum winds of 100 knots gusting to 120 knots, making it a major hurricane, though the chart does not plot wind radii so its precise threat area is not directly readable here. A second cold front trails across the Pacific Northwest into the northern Rockies, with a 1006 mb low along the coast of the Pacific Northwest driving that boundary, while the eastern seaboard sits under a broad 1004-1008 mb area with a frontal boundary draped across New England consistent with a slow-moving system there. The tightest pressure gradients on the chart are located around the Pacific Northwest low and across the Great Basin between the coastal low and the interior high, implying the strongest surface winds in those corridors.

sources.title: Canadian Surface Analysis
sources.summary: This CMC surface analysis valid 0000Z Monday 28 September 2026 shows a broad low pressure complex dominating central and eastern Canada, with a 999 hPa center positioned over what appears to be the Great Lakes or southern Ontario region and a 982 hPa low to its northwest over what the chart geometry suggests is the Hudson Bay or northern Ontario area, both connected by an active frontal zone trailing southward into the central United States. A strong 1033 hPa high is established over what appears to be James Bay or the eastern Hudson Bay area, producing a tight pressure gradient on its western flank where the isobars are noticeably compressed between it and the low centers to the west, implying a corridor of strong surface winds across portions of northern Quebec or Labrador. A 987 hPa low sits over the central Plains region of the United States with a cold front extending southward and a warm front pushing northeast, and the implied moisture and lift ahead of that system connect across the border into the Canadian Prairies or southern Manitoba where the isobar packing is moderate. Along the Pacific margin, a 1008 hPa low is analyzed near the British Columbia coast with a frontal boundary angling onshore, while the interior of western Canada sits under the influence of a 1024 to 1028 hPa high farther southwest, keeping that region relatively quiescent. The upper portion of the frame carries several Arctic lows near or beyond 70 degrees North that are unremarkable for that latitude and season, and no attempt is made here to place them over specific archipelago islands given the ambiguity of the polar projection at chart edges.

sources.title: 500 mb Analysis
sources.summary: At 500 mb valid 1200 UTC 28 September 2026, a deep longwave trough is centered over the central United States, with heights falling to near 558-564 dam over the central Plains and the trough axis oriented roughly north-south with a slight negative tilt, suggesting an amplified but still translationally active pattern rather than a fully blocked one. A large-amplitude ridge is evident across the Pacific Northwest and western Canada, with heights reaching 588-594 dam along the western edge of the domain, while a secondary ridge is building over the Gulf of Mexico near 588-590 dam beneath a labeled surface high, contributing to a high-amplitude, somewhat meridional flow pattern overall. The red L labeled over the western Atlantic, near the mid-Atlantic coast offshore, is associated with a closed 500 mb low based on the encircling height contours visible near 575-576 dam, making it a genuine cutoff low that has separated from the main westerlies and will tend to retrogress or stall rather than translate cleanly downstream. A broad implied jet corridor, consistent with the tight height gradient along the southern and eastern flanks of the central trough, appears to extend from the central Plains eastward into the Tennessee Valley and then curve northeastward toward the Atlantic cutoff, with wind barbs suggesting speeds of 60-80 knots across that corridor. The overall pattern — a western ridge, deep central trough, and eastern cutoff low — describes an amplified longwave configuration with reduced downstream progression, though the western ridge and central trough do not form a geometrically clean Rex or omega block.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB (GOES-19)
sources.summary: This GOES-19 AirMass RGB from 1331Z 28 September 2026 shows a well-defined tropical cyclone off the lower-left edge of the CONUS domain, positioned over the eastern Pacific off the Mexican coast, with a compact white-topped spiral and a clear eye visible. A broad expanse of orange-red coloring dominates the western and central CONUS from the Rockies eastward into the Plains, consistent with dry mid- to upper-tropospheric air under an upper ridge, but the uniform warm tone and lack of a compact elongated structure argue against a stratospheric intrusion here. The sharpest airmass boundary in the image runs as a narrow blue-green to orange transition in a roughly southwest-to-northeast arc from the central Plains into the Great Lakes region, marking the likely jet corridor separating the dry ridge air to the west from the cooler, drier upper-tropospheric air rendered in teal-blue to the northeast. Along and ahead of this boundary over the Tennessee Valley and lower Mississippi Valley, scattered clusters of white deep convective tops are visible, embedded in the green tropical-moist airmass streaming northward from the Gulf. A compact dry streamer, more saturated orange than the surrounding ridge air and with an elongated shape consistent with a cyclonic-flank intrusion, wraps into the circulation of the Pacific tropical cyclone on its poleward side.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB Full Disk (GOES-19)
sources.summary: This GOES-19 Air Mass RGB valid 28 September 2026 at 1320Z shows a broad green tropical airmass dominating from roughly 30N southward through the Amazon basin, with scattered clusters of bright white deep convective tops along the ITCZ axis across the eastern Pacific west of Central America and in isolated cells over the Colombian and Venezuelan interior. A distinct cyclonic swirl with dense white cold tops is visible in the eastern Pacific off the Mexican coast near roughly 15N, consistent with an organized tropical system. The transition to red-orange across the subtropical eastern Pacific and over northern South America reflects dry, subsident upper-tropospheric air under the subtropical ridge, not a stratospheric intrusion. In the Southern Hemisphere extratropics, a compact swirl of white cloud with a wrapped dry-air slot is visible near the southern tip of South America, indicating an active baroclinic system over the Drake Passage area. The upper portion of the disk over Canada and the Arctic shows a transition from green to dark blue-purple, marking the polar airmass boundary and implying the implied jet corridor runs across the upper tier of the CONUS and into the Atlantic, though the northern limb is partially cut off by the disk edge.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day Temperature Outlook
sources.summary: The dominant feature is a strongly above-normal signal centered over the interior Pacific Northwest and northern Great Basin, where the darkest brown shading indicates a 90-100% probability of above-normal temperatures across roughly central Oregon, Idaho, and Nevada, relaxing outward through 70-80% and 60-70% rings that still cover most of the West and reach into the central Plains by the October 3-7 window. This is the highest-confidence warm signal on the chart and, taken alongside the concentric probability structure, is consistent with a persistent or amplifying upper-level ridge anchored over the western interior. Countering that, a below-normal signal at 50-60% probability sits over Texas, Oklahoma, and portions of adjacent states, implying a downstream trough or at minimum a surface cold airmass in that sector, though the chart does not plot height or wind fields so that inference should be treated as implied rather than confirmed. The Southeast coast and Florida carry an above-normal signal at 60-70%, likely a separate influence from anomalous onshore flow or a lingering warm airmass that is geographically distinct from the western ridge. Alaska shows a split pattern with below-normal probabilities over the western portion of the state and above-normal along the southern coast and Panhandle, while Hawaii leans above normal at 40-50%, both consistent with a broader amplified Pacific pattern but too removed from the CONUS domain to constrain its structure further.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary:
This is indeed a CPC 6-10 day 500 mb height and anomaly forecast, valid 3-7 October 2026, with heights in dam (solid green, 60 m interval) and anomalies in dashed contours (red positive, blue negative).

The dominant feature is a strongly negative anomaly center over the Canadian Arctic Archipelago and into Hudson Bay, where the anomaly contours reach approximately -90 dam — that reading would be extraordinary and almost certainly reflects a misread or mislabeled contour; the values are more plausibly in the range of -9 dam, consistent with the deep closed low plotted near the Arctic Archipelago at around 500 dam. A broad positive anomaly area covers the Pacific and the western CONUS, with red dashed contours suggesting values near +30 to +40 in the same relative units across the southern tier and the subtropical Pacific, again best interpreted as roughly +3 to +4 dam departures. The ridge axis runs roughly north-south just west of the Canadian Rockies, with heights near 582-588 dam over the interior western United States, and the zero anomaly line appears to cross roughly through the central Plains, meaning positive anomalies do extend well into western North America but do not dominate east of roughly 100°W. The trough axis is displaced well north into the high Arctic rather than digging into the mid-latitudes, and the relatively zonal, widely-spaced height contours across the CONUS mid-latitudes are consistent with a pattern trending toward more amplified ridging in the west but with limited downstream troughing over the eastern half of the continent.

sources.title: CPC 8-14 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary:
This chart is a 500 mb height and height-anomaly forecast valid October 5–11, 2026, made September 27, 2026, so it is the 8–14 day product as described. The green solid contours are heights in dam at 60 dam intervals, with labeled values in the central domain reading approximately 540, 546, 552, 558, 564, 570, 574, and 582 dam, consistent with the expected 500–600 dam range for the mid-troposphere. The dashed contours are height anomalies, with red dashes positive and blue/purple dashes negative; the scale labels read in single to low double digits of dam, so the anomaly contours appear to be at roughly 3–9 dam intervals.

The dominant feature is a deep, positively tilted trough centered over the Canadian Arctic Archipelago and Hudson Bay, with heights at or below 540 dam near the center and a negative anomaly of roughly 6–9 dam implied by the clustering of blue dashed contours there. Western Canada, the northern Rockies, and the northern Plains do not show a positive height anomaly ridge core in this forecast; instead, the 552–558 dam height contours across the central and northern Plains are accompanied by near-zero or weakly negative anomaly contours, indicating below-normal or near-normal heights for that region. A ridge axis is present, but its core appears located well to the southwest, over the Desert Southwest and northern Mexico, where the 570–582 dam contours bow northward and positive anomaly contours (red dashes near +6 dam) are centered near the Four Corners–northern Mexico area — this is the retreated-ridge outcome, not a ridge still anchored over the northern Rockies. The eastern Pacific shows a second positive anomaly center off the Pacific Northwest coast, with positive red-dashed contours near +9 dam, while the eastern seaboard and western Atlantic carry weakly negative anomalies consistent with the trough's downstream amplification.

sources.title: WPC Short Range Forecast Discussion
sources.summary: A powerful Nor'easter near New Jersey brings coastal flooding, rip currents, strong winds, and heavy rain to the Mid-Atlantic and Northeast through Monday, then weakens and moves into the Gulf of Maine by Tuesday. Tropical moisture from Hurricane Polo produces widespread heavy rain across the Southwest, Great Basin, and Central/Southern Rockies Monday through Wednesday with considerable flash flooding expected across New Mexico and western Texas. Moderate Risk excessive rainfall issued for multiple areas across the Southwest and High Plains. Upper Midwest faces Slight Risk excessive rainfall Monday into Tuesday from a Northern Plains low pressure system. Severe thunderstorms with wind, hail, and tornadoes possible over Southern Plains Wednesday.

sources.title: SPC Day 1 Convective Outlook
sources.summary: No severe thunderstorm areas are forecast for Day 1 (valid through 29/1200Z). Over the Northern Plains, scattered to isolated thunderstorms are expected as a surface trough focuses activity amid modest CAPE (500-1500 J/kg) and forcing. While some strong storms are possible, uncertainty regarding location and intensity precludes low-end severe probabilities. A southerly low-level jet may reinvigorate storms overnight. In Southeast California through western Arizona, numerous showers and thunderstorms are expected ahead of a mid-level shortwave trough, but widespread cloud cover and weak mid-level lapse rates limit instability. A stronger storm is possible but the threat remains too low to warrant probabilities.

sources.title: SPC Mesoscale Discussions
sources.summary: No organized convective threat is currently being monitored by SPC. No mesoscale discussions have been issued in the past 6 hours.

sources.title: NHC Tropical Weather Outlooks
sources.summary:
ATLANTIC: Tropical Depression Fay active southwest of Azores. Low pressure system east-northeast of Bermuda organizing and moving eastward; likely becomes tropical depression or storm within 1-2 days as it turns southeast and slows. High formation probability (70% through 48 hours, 80% through 7 days) despite currently marginal conditions; conditions deteriorate later in week.

EAST PACIFIC: Three active systems — Hurricane Polo near Cabo San Lazaro, Hurricane Nolo southwest of Hawaiian Islands, Tropical Storm Rachel south-southwest of Acapulco. Broad low pressure well east-southeast of Hawaii becoming better organized in conducive conditions; tropical depression expected to form today or tomorrow, moving northeastward away from islands. High formation probability (90% both timeframes).

sources.title: ENSO State (Oceanic Niño Index)
sources.summary: The Oceanic Niño Index shows La Niña conditions currently (NDJ 2025 at -0.60 anomaly), with the cold phase weakening through early 2026. By late winter/early spring, the index transitions to neutral and then warm conditions, reaching +1.80 anomaly by summer 2026 (JJA). This indicates an expected shift from La Niña toward El Niño over the next several months.

sources.title: Teleconnection Indices (PNA, AO, NAO)
sources.summary: PNA remains modestly negative (-0.34, 7-day mean -0.58), showing little trend. AO is near zero (latest +0.53, 7-day mean +0.00) after recent swings between positive and negative values. NAO has fallen notably to -0.66 (7-day mean -1.01 versus prior -0.51), strengthening its negative phase over the past week. Given summer's weak teleconnection signals, these indices provide directional guidance rather than strong constraints. The NAO's shift toward negative values may support retention of eastern cutoff patterns.
